issues.subcategory: Inconsistent p-value reporting for sadness variable
issues.description: In the Results section for Primary Analysis 1, the chi-square test for sad words is reported as χ²(3)=8.74, p=.003. However, in Table 2, the same test shows p=.033. These two p-values are mutually inconsistent for the same test statistic and degrees of freedom. A chi-square value of 8.74 with 3 df yields p≈.033, making the in-text p=.003 incorrect. This discrepancy affects interpretation of the significance of this finding.
issues.quote: there was a significant effect of episode type on use of sad words, 2(3)=8.74, p=.003

issues.subcategory: Inconsistent p-value for anger interaction
issues.description: In Table 3, the anger interaction p-value for Attempt vs. Positive is reported as p=.011 (with the value written as .0111 in the text), while the text states p=.011. The value .0111 appears to be a typographical artifact but also raises questions about rounding conventions applied inconsistently across the table. More importantly, the chi-square for the anger interaction is χ²(3)=7.83, p=.049, which is borderline significant and particularly sensitive to multiple comparison concerns given the number of tests run.
issues.quote: Episode type (Attempt vs. Positive) × Time | | | | -0.027 | 0.011 | z=-2.54 | .0111

issues.subcategory: Sign direction inconsistency in interaction coefficients
issues.description: For positive emotion, the interaction betas are positive (e.g., β=0.010, 0.027, 0.016), yet the text states 'positive emotion decreased more steeply during attempt episodes.' In a GLMM with logit link where day ranges from -14 to 0 (approaching the attempt), a positive interaction coefficient for Attempt vs. Other × Time would mean positive emotion decreases less steeply (or increases more) in attempt episodes relative to comparison episodes, not more steeply. The sign of the coefficients appears inconsistent with the narrative interpretation, suggesting either a coding error in how 'day' was parameterized or an error in interpreting the direction of the interaction.
issues.quote: there was a significant interaction for positive emotion, 2(3)=41.67, p<.001, such that positive emotion decreased more steeply during attempt episodes compared to all other episode types

issues.subcategory: Sign direction inconsistency for anger interaction coefficients
issues.description: Similarly, for anger, the interaction betas are all negative (e.g., β=-0.023, -0.026, -0.027), yet the text states 'anger increased more steeply during attempt compared to all other episode types.' With day coded from -14 to 0, negative interaction coefficients for Attempt vs. Other × Time would indicate that anger increases less steeply (or decreases more) in attempt episodes relative to comparisons, contradicting the stated interpretation. This sign inconsistency is present for multiple variables and suggests a systematic error in either the coding of the time variable or the interpretation of model output.
issues.quote: There was also a significant interaction for anger words, such that anger increased more steeply during attempt compared to all other episode types

issues.subcategory: Significant omnibus test with no significant pairwise comparisons for death words
issues.description: The omnibus interaction for death words is reported as significant (χ²(3)=9.47, p=.024), yet none of the pairwise comparisons reach significance (ps=.067-.739). The authors note this but do not adequately explain the discrepancy. This pattern—a significant omnibus F/chi-square with no significant pairwise tests—suggests the omnibus test may be driven by a comparison not directly tested (e.g., ideation vs. depressed or ideation vs. positive), or that the omnibus test is a false positive. Reporting a significant interaction without any significant follow-up comparisons is misleading and the authors' interpretation that 'ideation episodes appeared to show a steeper decrease in death words' is post-hoc and unsupported by formal tests.
issues.quote: There was also a significant interaction for death words, 2(3)=9.47, p=.024. However, there were no significant differences in change over time for attempt compared to all other episodes (zs=0.33-1.83, ps=.067-.739)

issues.subcategory: Mixed use of z and t statistics without clear justification
issues.description: The emotional tone variable uses t-statistics for pairwise comparisons (e.g., t=4.27, t=1.48, t=0.86) while all other sentiment variables use z-statistics. The authors note that LMMs use 'lmer' with t-statistics and GLMMs use 'glmer' with z-statistics, but no degrees of freedom are reported for the t-tests, making it impossible to evaluate their significance. Without degrees of freedom, the p-values for t-statistics cannot be verified. This is a known issue with lme4 (which does not compute p-values for t-statistics by default), and the method used to derive p-values from t-statistics is not disclosed.
issues.quote: Episode type (Attempt vs. Depressed) × Time | | | | 0.401 | 0.094 | t=4.27 | <.001

issues.subcategory: Power analysis based on between-subjects effect sizes applied to within-subjects design
issues.description: The power analysis uses effect sizes from between-subjects studies (ds=1.06-1.52) to justify the sample size for a within-subjects design. The authors acknowledge this limitation briefly but still use these estimates as the basis for their power calculation. Within-subjects effect sizes can differ substantially from between-subjects effect sizes, and the direction of this difference is unknown. Furthermore, the power analysis references 'Cramer's V=0.29' as the detectable effect size for chi-square tests, but the primary analyses use mixed-effects models, not chi-square tests, making the power calculation methodology mismatched to the actual analytic approach.
issues.quote: We determined that a sample size of 30 suicide attempters (representing 60 attempts but only 20 with collected, usable SMS data, divided by the design effect) would provide enough power to detect only large effect sizes (Cramer's V=0.29) for chi-square tests of mixed-effects models

issues.subcategory: Incorrect description of beta coefficients as effect sizes in log-odds units
issues.description: The authors state that 'β (standardized values of the model parameter estimates in log odds units) are reported and serve as effect sizes.' This is internally contradictory: log-odds units are unstandardized, while standardized coefficients are dimensionless. The betas reported in the tables appear to be unstandardized log-odds coefficients, not standardized effect sizes. Calling them 'standardized' is incorrect and misleading, as it implies comparability across variables that are on different scales.
issues.quote: β (standardized values of the model parameter estimates in log odds units) are reported and serve as effect sizes

issues.subcategory: No pre-registration; extensive undisclosed researcher degrees of freedom
issues.description: The study is not pre-registered, and the authors acknowledge that 'numerous aspects of this research were exploratory by nature.' The choice of a two-week episode window was made both theoretically and empirically ('The question of the optimal time window was also assessed empirically, using visual inspection of descriptive figures'), meaning the window was selected after examining the data. This constitutes a researcher degree of freedom that inflates Type I error. The decision to not apply multiple comparison corrections is also made post-hoc and justified by citing a single methodological opinion paper (Rothman, 1990), without acknowledging that this decision was made after observing the pattern of results.
issues.quote: The decision to set each episode at two weeks long was made in a conservative effort to capture the critical period... The question of the optimal time window was also assessed empirically, using visual inspection of descriptive figures

issues.subcategory: Post-hoc decision not to correct for multiple comparisons
issues.description: The authors ran a large number of statistical tests across two primary analyses (at least 14 omnibus tests plus numerous pairwise comparisons) without applying any correction for multiple comparisons. The justification—that this is a pilot study and they did not want to 'artificially suppress Type I error'—is made after observing the results and is not a pre-specified analytic decision. The Rothman (1990) citation is a controversial opinion piece, not a methodological consensus. Given that several key findings (anger interaction: p=.049; positive emotion vs. ideation: p=.049; self-focus vs. depressed: p=.035) are at or near the uncorrected α=.05 threshold, a Bonferroni or FDR correction would likely render these non-significant.
issues.quote: we decided not to artificially suppress Type I error (i.e., using a multiple comparisons correction) but rather view any significant results in light of these caveats

issues.subcategory: Undisclosed supplementary analyses examining robustness
issues.description: The authors mention 'Additional analyses were performed to examine the same set of outcome variables but in different ways to examine the robustness of the primary results' but relegate these entirely to a supplement without describing the criteria for what would constitute a 'robust' vs. 'non-robust' finding, or how discrepancies between primary and supplementary analyses would be handled. This creates an undisclosed researcher degree of freedom in which the primary results could be selectively reported based on which analytic approach yielded significant results.
issues.quote: Condition comparisons using alternate data subsets. Additional analyses were performed to examine the same set of outcome variables but in different ways to examine the robustness of the primary results and to see if the pattern of results changed.

issues.subcategory: Retrospective episode identification with potential memory bias
issues.description: The entire study design depends on participants retrospectively identifying the dates of past suicide attempts and other episodes, sometimes from years prior. While the authors acknowledge this limitation, they understate its severity. Memory for the precise timing of emotional episodes is known to be unreliable, and the dates of suicide attempts may be subject to telescoping, reconstruction, and motivated distortion. The authors report that 90.3% of episodes were rated as 'very certain' or 'somewhat certain,' but 'somewhat certain' explicitly means 'may be off by a few days,' which is highly consequential for a study examining day-by-day language changes in a 14-day window.
issues.quote: Participants were generally confident about the accuracy of the dates they selected, rating 90.3% of episodes as 'very certain' (i.e., exact days) or 'somewhat certain' (i.e., may be off by a few days).

issues.subcategory: Absence of blinding in episode classification
issues.description: The experimenter who conducted the clinical interview to classify episodes was not blinded to the study hypotheses. The interview was used to classify episodes into risk categories (attempt, ideation, depressed, positive), which then served as the primary predictor variable. Without blinding, there is risk that the experimenter's probing questions and classification decisions were influenced by knowledge of the hypotheses, potentially biasing episode classification in ways that favor the expected results.
issues.quote: During the interview, participants were asked to identify a number of specific events or episodes in the past and the calendar dates during which the episodes took place.

issues.subcategory: Highly selective data availability undermining within-subjects design
issues.description: Only 134 of 293 collected episodes (46%) contained SMS data, from only 27 of 33 participants. The authors do not report whether data availability was systematically related to episode type, recency, or participant characteristics. If, for example, attempt episodes were more likely to be recent (and thus more likely to have available SMS data), or if participants with more severe histories were more or less likely to have data, the within-subjects design is compromised. The pattern of missingness is not described in sufficient detail to evaluate this threat.
issues.quote: Among the episodes queried during the lab interview, 134 (46%) episodes contained SMS data, collected from 27 different participants.

issues.subcategory: Inconsistent episode length between attempt and other episode types
issues.description: The methods describe suicide attempt episodes as using 'the one-week period prior to the attempt' while all other episode types (ideation, depressed, positive) are defined as 'two-week episodes.' However, the analyses describe examining 'the 14 days leading up to a suicide attempt' and the day variable ranges from -14 to 0. This is internally inconsistent: if attempt episodes are one week long, the temporal analysis cannot examine 14 days of data for attempt episodes. This inconsistency is never resolved and fundamentally affects the comparability of episode types in the slope analyses.
issues.quote: past actual, interrupted, or aborted suicide attempts, using the one-week period prior to the attempt as a 'suicide attempt episode'... two-week episodes of suicide ideation... two-week episodes of depressed mood... two-week episode of typical mood

issues.subcategory: Random effects structure reduced due to non-convergence without sensitivity analysis
issues.description: For the slope analyses (Primary Analysis 2), the authors state that 'Models with the full set of random slopes did not converge; therefore, no random slopes were included in the final model.' This is a substantial departure from the maximal random effects structure recommended by Barr et al. (2013) and used in Analysis 1. Removing all random slopes when the maximal model fails to converge is one approach, but it is not the only or necessarily best approach. No sensitivity analyses comparing different random effects structures are reported, and the authors do not discuss how this decision may have inflated Type I error rates in Analysis 2 specifically.
issues.quote: Models with the full set of random slopes did not converge; therefore, no random slopes were included in the final model.

issues.subcategory: Heterogeneous definition of suicide attempt episode
issues.description: The study includes 'actual, interrupted, or aborted suicide attempts' under a single 'attempt' episode category. These represent meaningfully different levels of behavioral enactment: an aborted attempt (deciding not to act) is categorically different from an enacted attempt (taking pills). The authors acknowledge that 71% of incidents did not result in any physical harm. Collapsing these into a single 'high risk' category introduces substantial heterogeneity and may dilute or distort any signal. The authors briefly acknowledge this but do not report sensitivity analyses separating enacted from non-enacted attempts.
issues.quote: 29% of incidents involved some action being taken in which some physical harm was caused... while 71% of incidents did not result in any physical harm

issues.subcategory: First-person pronoun use as operationalization of self-focus/rumination
issues.description: The authors operationalize 'self-focus' and 'rumination' using singular first-person pronoun use ('I' words) from LIWC. However, first-person pronoun use in text messages is heavily influenced by the pragmatics of the communication context (e.g., making plans, describing one's own actions, expressing opinions) and does not necessarily reflect ruminative self-focus. Text messages are inherently first-person communications, making the baseline rate of 'I' usage very high and potentially insensitive to the psychological construct of interest. The validity of this operationalization for text message data specifically has not been established.
issues.quote: we tested whether use of first-person pronouns (as an indicator of rumination) was greater prior to suicide attempts

issues.subcategory: Social engagement operationalized only as message volume ratios
issues.description: The interpersonal theory of suicide posits thwarted belongingness and perceived burdensomeness as key constructs. The authors operationalize 'social engagement' solely as the ratio of sent vs. received messages and word counts. This is a very distal and indirect measure of the theoretical constructs. Message volume ratios do not capture the quality of social interactions, the emotional content of social exchanges, whether the person feels connected or burdened, or whether they are withdrawing from specific relationships. The authors acknowledge this in the discussion but do not adequately address the construct validity problem in the methods.
issues.quote: we tested whether suicide attempters demonstrated greater signs of disengagement from and burdensomeness on their social support networks prior to suicide attempts compared to other episodes by examining patterns in outgoing vs. incoming messages

issues.subcategory: LIWC not validated for SMS text message genre
issues.description: LIWC was developed and validated primarily on longer-form text (essays, diary entries, social media posts). SMS text messages are a distinct linguistic genre characterized by abbreviations, emoji, non-standard spelling, very short length, and highly context-dependent meaning. The authors do not discuss whether LIWC has been validated for SMS data or whether its word categories perform equivalently in this genre. The note that 'not happy' would be counted as positive emotion (negation not handled) is particularly problematic for short messages where such constructions are common.
issues.quote: One weakness of this approach is that examining single words in isolation can fail to capture the semantic context of the word (e.g., 'not happy' would count as 'positive emotion' because negation is not accounted for)

issues.subcategory: Causal language used for correlational retrospective findings
issues.description: Throughout the paper, the authors use causal and predictive language ('predicted suicide attempt,' 'markers of suicide risk,' 'identify when someone is at imminent risk') for findings derived from a retrospective correlational design. The study cannot establish that language patterns caused or preceded suicide attempts in a causal sense, nor can it establish predictive validity in a prospective sense. The retrospective identification of episodes means that the 'prediction' is actually post-diction—the language data are being examined after the outcome is already known.
issues.quote: By reconstructing the timeline of recent suicidal behaviors through a retrospective clinical interview, we utilized a prospective research design to understand which features in text communications predicted suicide attempt

issues.subcategory: Unaddressed confounds between episode types
issues.description: The comparison between episode types (attempt vs. ideation vs. depressed vs. positive) is confounded by numerous variables that are not controlled for: time period (more recent episodes may have more SMS data and different communication patterns due to secular trends in texting behavior), life circumstances (episodes may differ in relationship status, employment, academic stress), treatment status (participants may have been in treatment during some episodes but not others), and medication effects. None of these potential confounds are measured or controlled in the analyses.
issues.quote: We performed inferential analyses using mixed-effects models to examine within-subject (between-episode) differences among suicide attempters in several communication features.

issues.subcategory: Reverse causality not addressed
issues.description: The authors assume that language patterns change as a function of increasing suicide risk. However, reverse causality is possible: changes in communication patterns (e.g., receiving fewer messages, having more conflict in text exchanges) could contribute to increasing suicide risk rather than merely reflecting it. The correlational and retrospective design cannot distinguish between these causal directions, yet the paper consistently frames language as a marker or predictor of risk rather than acknowledging bidirectional possibilities.
issues.quote: Results suggest private electronic communication has the potential to provide real-time digital markers of suicide risk.

issues.subcategory: Contradiction between abstract and results regarding mean differences
issues.description: The abstract states 'no language features uniquely differentiated suicide attempts from other episodes' for mean differences. However, the results section reports a significant effect of episode type on sad words (χ²(3)=8.74, p=.003/.033) with a significant pairwise comparison between attempt and ideation episodes (z=-2.64, p=.008). The discussion then states 'results indicated that the period of high risk just before a suicide attempt was associated with messages indicating greater anxiety and sadness.' The abstract's claim of 'no' differences contradicts the reported significant sadness finding, and the discussion introduces anxiety as significant when no significant anxiety effect was reported in the results.
issues.quote: Regarding mean differences, no language features uniquely differentiated suicide attempts from other episodes... results indicated that the period of high risk just before a suicide attempt was associated with messages indicating greater anxiety and sadness

issues.subcategory: Discrepancy in number of attempts with SMS data
issues.description: The results section states '13 participants reported a single lifetime attempt and 14 reported multiple (M=1.74, SD=0.86)' among attempters with SMS data, totaling 27 participants. However, it then states 'Among the 21 attempts with corresponding SMS data.' If 13 participants had one attempt and 14 had multiple (average 1.74), the expected number of attempts would be 13×1 + 14×1.74 ≈ 37, not 21. This numerical inconsistency is unexplained and raises questions about how 'attempts with SMS data' was defined versus 'participants with SMS data.'
issues.quote: Among attempters with SMS data, 13 participants reported a single lifetime attempt and 14 reported multiple (M=1.74, SD=0.86). Among the 21 attempts with corresponding SMS data

issues.subcategory: Contradiction in episode length between methods sections
issues.description: The interview section states suicide attempt episodes use 'the one-week period prior to the attempt,' but the Overview and Hypotheses section states 'two weeks before a suicide attempt' and the slope analysis uses 'day of episode (numerical factor ranging from -14 to 0).' The abstract also refers to 'two weeks before a suicide attempt.' This inconsistency about whether attempt episodes are one week or two weeks long is never resolved and is fundamental to understanding what data were actually analyzed.
issues.quote: past actual, interrupted, or aborted suicide attempts, using the one-week period prior to the attempt as a 'suicide attempt episode'

issues.subcategory: Iatrogenic effects result contradicts stated direction
issues.description: The iatrogenic effects analysis reports that 'desire to die from pre (M=0.82, SD=1.10) to post (M=1.03, SD=0.90) significantly decreased slightly, t(32)=2.23, p=.033.' However, the means show an increase from 0.82 to 1.03, not a decrease. The t-statistic and p-value indicate a significant change, but the direction stated ('decreased') contradicts the reported means. This is either a reporting error in the means or in the stated direction of change.
issues.quote: desire to die from pre (M=0.82, SD=1.10) to post (M=1.03, SD=0.90) significantly decreased slightly, t(32)=2.23, p=.033

issues.subcategory: Missing degrees of freedom for t-statistics in mixed models
issues.description: For the emotional tone variable analyzed with LMM, t-statistics are reported (e.g., t=4.27, t=1.48, t=0.86) without degrees of freedom. The lme4 package does not compute degrees of freedom for t-statistics by default, and the method used to derive p-values (e.g., Satterthwaite approximation, Kenward-Roger, likelihood ratio test, or normal approximation) is not disclosed. Without this information, the reported p-values cannot be verified or evaluated.
issues.quote: Episode type (Attempt vs. Depressed) × Time | | | | 0.401 | 0.094 | t=4.27 | <.001

issues.subcategory: Missing information about SMS data coverage relative to episode dates
issues.description: The study does not report what proportion of episode days had at least one text message, or the distribution of message counts per day within episodes. Given that the slope analyses examine day-by-day changes over 14 days, it is critical to know how many days within each episode had zero messages (true zeros vs. missing data) and how this varied by episode type. Days with no messages could reflect social withdrawal (theoretically meaningful) or simply days when the participant did not text (not meaningful), and these cannot be distinguished.
issues.quote: Across all episodes, 189,478 text messages were collected and analyzed, ranging between on average about 1,200-1,600 text messages per episode.

issues.subcategory: No reporting of model fit statistics or random effects variance components
issues.description: The mixed-effects models are described and results of fixed effects are reported, but no information is provided about random effects variance components (e.g., variance of random intercepts for participant, episode, message), intraclass correlations, or model fit statistics. These are essential for evaluating the appropriateness of the model structure and the degree of clustering in the data. Without this information, readers cannot assess whether the random effects structure was appropriate or whether the models converged properly.
issues.quote: A random by-participant slope for episode type and random intercepts of participant, participant-episode, and message were included as the random effects.

issues.subcategory: Missing description of how LIWC scores were aggregated across messages within days
issues.description: The slope analyses examine day-level changes, but LIWC scores are computed at the individual message level. The paper does not describe how message-level LIWC scores were aggregated to the day level for the temporal analyses, or whether the mixed model analyzed message-level data with day as a continuous predictor. If message-level data were used, the nesting structure (messages within days within episodes within participants) is more complex than described, and the random effects structure may be inadequate.
issues.quote: A series of mixed-effects models were performed for each language feature with 3 fixed effects: episode type (4 levels: attempt, ideation, depressed, positive), day of episode (numerical factor ranging from -14 to 0), and the interaction of episode type and day.

issues.subcategory: Supplementary materials not accessible for review
issues.description: Multiple critical pieces of information are relegated to supplementary materials that are not included in the manuscript: the CONSORT diagram (Figure S1), descriptive episode information (Supplement 1), additional mixed-effects model information (Supplement 2), robustness analyses (Supplement 3), and specific LIWC variables used (Table S3). The specific LIWC variables used to operationalize each construct are particularly important for replication and are not described in the main text.
issues.quote: see Table S3 for the specific LIWC variables calculated for the three psychological constructs

issues.subcategory: Highly homogeneous sample limits generalizability
issues.description: The sample is 84.8% female, 60.6% White, 94% with 'some college' education, and has a mean age of 20.4 years, recruited from a university participant pool. This is an extremely narrow demographic profile. Suicide rates and risk factors differ substantially by sex (males are 4x more likely to die by suicide), age, and socioeconomic status. The authors acknowledge the sex imbalance briefly in the limitations but do not adequately address how this affects generalizability of the language-based findings, particularly given that communication styles and texting behavior differ substantially by sex and age.
issues.quote: Most of the participants were female, White, and college-aged.

issues.subcategory: Overclaiming real-time clinical applicability from retrospective pilot data
issues.description: The paper repeatedly claims that findings could lead to 'real-time digital markers of suicide risk' and 'an objective monitoring tool capable of tracking individuals' communication behind the scenes.' These claims substantially overstate what can be concluded from a retrospective pilot study with N=33 (27 with usable data) that has not been validated prospectively. The sensitivity and specificity of any potential monitoring tool are completely unknown from this study, and the clinical utility claims are premature.
issues.quote: Knowledge gained from this study could put us one step closer to the development of an objective monitoring tool capable of tracking individuals' communication 'behind the scenes,' notifying suicidal individuals and/or their clinician or family if their patterns of communication indicate increasing levels of suicide risk.

issues.subcategory: Missing data mechanism not evaluated for SMS availability
issues.description: Only 46% of episodes had SMS data. The authors describe practical reasons for missing data (encryption settings, old phones, cloud backup issues) but do not formally test whether data availability was related to episode type, participant characteristics, or episode recency. If SMS data were more likely to be available for recent episodes, and if recent episodes were more likely to be attempt episodes (since participants were recruited based on recent attempt history), this could systematically bias the sample of episodes with data in ways that affect the results.
issues.quote: a number of iPhone users had encryption settings on their phones that prevented third-party iPhone software from accessing text data... many participants did not know whether they had laptop or cloud backups

issues.subcategory: Unequal episode representation across participants not adequately addressed
issues.description: Participants contributed between 3 and 12 episodes, and 'Participants reported and had SMS data for on average approximately 1.5 episodes for each episode type.' This means some participants contributed data for only one or two episode types, severely limiting the within-subjects comparisons for those individuals. The mixed-effects model handles this through random effects, but the degree to which the within-subjects design is actually achieved (i.e., how many participants contributed data for all four episode types) is not reported.
issues.quote: A total of 3 to 12 episodes were collected for each participant depending on the presence and number of reported events.

issues.subcategory: Misapplication of escape theory to predict text message content
issues.description: Baumeister's (1990) escape theory predicts that suicidal individuals seek to escape self-awareness, which would theoretically lead to cognitive deconstruction and reduced self-focused thought—not increased self-focus. The authors cite this theory to predict increased self-focus prior to suicide attempts, but the theory actually predicts the opposite: that the escape from self-awareness would reduce self-focused cognition. The authors conflate the antecedent state (painful self-awareness leading to the desire to escape) with the escape state itself, misapplying the theoretical prediction.
issues.quote: one theory of suicide posits that suicide is a means to escape from negative self-focus (Baumeister, 1990). It follows that the feedback loop of increasing self-focus and painful recognition of self-failures may lead someone to act on their suicidal thoughts

issues.subcategory: Conflation of between-subjects and within-subjects theoretical predictions
issues.description: The theoretical predictions and prior empirical support cited throughout the introduction are based on between-subjects comparisons (suicidal vs. non-suicidal individuals). The authors apply these between-subjects findings to generate within-subjects hypotheses (how language changes within the same person across different risk states). This is a fundamental theoretical leap that is not justified. A person's baseline level of self-focus or negative emotion may be stable across episodes, with only the trajectory changing, making between-subjects effect sizes irrelevant to within-subjects predictions.
issues.quote: Although no studies to date have examined text messaging content or any other private (i.e., not publicly available) electronic personal communications, we had several hypotheses based on the psychological theories of suicide previously discussed.

issues.subcategory: Absence of control group or normative comparison
issues.description: The study uses only suicide attempters and compares different episode types within this group. There is no non-clinical control group to establish baseline texting patterns. This means it is impossible to determine whether the language patterns observed during 'positive mood' episodes in suicide attempters are similar to or different from those of non-suicidal individuals, which would be important for understanding the specificity of any identified markers. The within-subjects design, while innovative, cannot address whether the identified patterns are specific to suicide risk or reflect general emotional dysregulation in a high-risk population.
issues.quote: A sample of 33 participants with at least one reported past suicide attempt were recruited from the Charlottesville community.

issues.subcategory: Uncontrolled variation in texting platform and communication norms
issues.description: The study collected only SMS text messages, but participants may have used other messaging platforms (iMessage, WhatsApp, Snapchat, Instagram DMs) for a substantial portion of their communication. The proportion of total communication captured by SMS likely varied substantially across participants and may have changed over time (secular trend toward app-based messaging). If participants shifted away from SMS toward other platforms during certain episode types or time periods, the SMS data would be an increasingly unrepresentative sample of their communication.
issues.quote: Additional forms of personal digital data, including phone call history, Google data (Gmail, Hangouts, and Chrome browser history), Facebook messages, and Twitter messages, were collected for the purposes of future analyses but are not part of the current study.
